title: MODULE 01 — Web Architecture and Frontend Engineering Foundations

overview.text: This module establishes the technical foundation required to become a frontend engineer. Before learning HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, or frontend frameworks, you need to understand what happens when someone enters a website address, how the browser communicates with servers, how web pages are constructed, and how frontend applications are developed and maintained.
The objective is not simply to learn terminology. It is to understand the complete journey from a user's browser request to the webpage appearing on the screen.
Understand how the web works before building applications.

Modern frontend engineering involves much more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. A frontend engineer must understand how browsers communicate with servers, how web applications are delivered over the internet, how the browser processes resources, and how development tools help engineers build, inspect, debug, and maintain applications.
This module introduces the architecture behind modern websites and establishes the foundation for advanced frontend development.
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

items: Explain the evolution and fundamental architecture of the World Wide Web.
Describe how the internet connects computers and how web applications use that infrastructure.
Understand client-server architecture and the responsibilities of each component.
Explain HTTP, HTTPS, headers, methods, status codes, and the request-response lifecycle.
Describe DNS resolution, domain names, hosting, and how websites become accessible.
Explain how browsers download, parse, render, and display web pages.
Understand the DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, painting, and compositing.
Configure a frontend development environment and use browser developer tools.
Use Git and GitHub to manage frontend projects and collaborate with other developers.
Inspect network activity and rendering behavior in an actual website.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — Evolution of the World Wide Web

blocks.text: 1.1 What Is the World Wide Web?
The World Wide Web (WWW) is a system of interconnected documents, applications, and resources that people access through the internet.
It allows users to navigate between websites, read information, view images, watch videos, interact with applications, and communicate with remote servers.
The web primarily relies on three foundational technologies:
HTML defines the structure and meaning of content on a webpage.
CSS controls how HTML elements look and how they are arranged.

items: Layout systems such as Flexbox and Grid.

blocks.text: JavaScript makes web pages interactive and dynamic.

items: Update page content without a full reload.

blocks.text: Together, these technologies form the foundation of frontend development.
1.2 Difference Between the Internet and the Web
The internet and the World Wide Web are related, but they are not the same thing.
**The internet** is the global network infrastructure that connects computers, servers, mobile devices, and other systems.
**The World Wide Web** is one of the services that operates on top of this network.

items: Email can operate through internet protocols without using the web.
Online gaming uses the internet to exchange information.
File transfers can use internet protocols.
Websites use the web through browsers and technologies such as HTTP and HTTPS.

blocks.text: Think of the internet as the transportation infrastructure and the web as one service that uses it.
The web has changed significantly since its creation.
The earliest generation of websites was mainly designed to distribute information.

items: Content primarily published by website owners.

blocks.text: An early company website might contain its history, address, contact information, and product descriptions. Visitors could read the information but had few ways to interact with the website.
Web 2.0 — The Interactive and Social Web
Web 2.0 describes the transition toward highly interactive websites and platforms where users actively create and exchange content.
A user can now upload videos, publish articles, write comments, send messages, and interact with other users through a browser.
Web 3.0 — A Term With Multiple Interpretations
Web 3.0 has been used to describe different ideas.
One interpretation focuses on the Semantic Web: making information more understandable and connected through structured data and machine-readable relationships.
Another popular interpretation describes decentralized applications built using blockchain technologies, smart contracts, and distributed networks.
These interpretations are not identical, and the term does not have one universally accepted technical definition.
Frontend engineers may encounter Web 3.0 technologies when building decentralized application interfaces, connecting wallets, or interacting with smart contracts.
Modern websites are no longer simply collections of static documents.

items: Content delivery networks distributing static resources.

blocks.text: A student opens the platform and:
Each action may involve communication between frontend code, backend APIs, databases, authentication services, and external systems.
The frontend provides the user experience, but the complete application depends on several interconnected technologies.
1.5 Why This Matters for Frontend Engineers
Understanding the evolution of the web helps developers understand why modern frontend development requires more than writing markup and styles.

items: How different frontend architectures solve different problems.

blocks.text: Imagine a course dashboard displaying a student's progress.
The frontend may request information from an API:
The backend retrieves progress information and returns a response. JavaScript then updates the interface to display completed lessons and remaining modules.
This is a modern web application in action.

sections.title: LESSON 02 — How the Internet and Web Applications Work

blocks.text: The internet is a worldwide system of interconnected networks.
Computers and other devices communicate through standardized networking protocols that define how information should be addressed, transmitted, and received.
A device connected to the internet may communicate with:
The communication is not based on physical proximity. Two devices on opposite sides of the world can exchange information through interconnected networks.
An Internet Protocol (IP) address is a network address used to identify an interface on an IP network.
When a device communicates over an IP network, IP addressing helps information reach the intended destination.
There are two widely used IP versions.
An IPv4 address contains 32 bits and is commonly written as four decimal numbers separated by periods.
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and provides a substantially larger address space.
IPv6 was developed partly to address the limited address availability of IPv4.
Not every device needs a unique public IPv4 address. Private addressing and network address translation (NAT) allow multiple devices to share a public address.
2.3 How Data Travels Across the Internet
When your computer sends information to a remote server, that information travels through multiple networking components.
A simplified communication path may include:

items: Your local router or network gateway.

blocks.text: Routers examine packet destination addresses and forward packets toward their destinations.
Information is generally transmitted in packets rather than as one uninterrupted physical message.
Protocols define how packets are addressed, delivered, checked, and reassembled.
IP provides addressing and packet-routing functionality.
It helps packets travel from their source toward their destination.
IP itself does not guarantee that every packet arrives successfully or in the correct order.
TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream communication.
TCP is widely used by applications that need reliable communication.
UDP provides a simpler datagram-based communication mechanism.
It does not provide TCP-style guarantees for delivery or ordering.
Applications that use UDP may implement additional reliability mechanisms themselves.
It is useful in systems where low communication overhead or application-controlled delivery behavior is important.
QUIC is a modern transport protocol built over UDP.
It provides features such as encrypted communication, multiplexed streams, and faster connection establishment in appropriate circumstances.
An IP address identifies a network destination, while a port number helps identify the application or service receiving the communication.

items: Port 80 is the default port associated with HTTP.
Port 443 is the default port associated with HTTPS.
Port 22 is commonly used by SSH.
Port 53 is commonly used by DNS.

blocks.text: A server can run several network services using different ports.
For example, one server may provide a website over HTTPS while also accepting administrative SSH connections.
2.6 What Happens When You Open a Website?

items: It determines the destination hostname and required protocol.
It obtains the destination IP address through DNS resolution if needed.
It establishes the required network connection.
For HTTPS, it establishes secure communication using TLS.
The server returns an HTTP response.
The browser processes the returned content.

blocks.text: In real applications, this sequence may involve redirects, proxies, caching, service workers, CDNs, multiple server requests, and additional browser processes.
A typical web application contains several components.
The frontend is the part of the application that users interact with.
Technologies include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, and other frontend frameworks.
The backend handles application functionality that runs outside the browser.
An API provides a defined way for different software components to communicate.
For example, a frontend might request a user's course list from a backend API.
The API defines the request structure, response format, authentication requirements, and expected behavior.
Consider a student visiting a learning platform.
The browser requests the frontend application.
The browser downloads the required HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other resources.
The frontend uses the available authentication mechanism to determine whether the user has an active session.
The application sends a request to the backend:
The backend validates the request and retrieves the relevant course information.
JavaScript processes the response and displays the course information.
This demonstrates how internet infrastructure, frontend code, backend services, and databases work together.
Client-server architecture is a computing model in which one system requests services or resources from another system.
The requesting system is called the client.
The system providing the requested service is called the server.

items: A browser commonly acts as the client.
A web server receives and processes requests.
Backend application code performs business operations.
A database stores and retrieves information.

blocks.text: The client-server model is one of the central foundations of web application architecture.
A client is an application or device that requests services from another system.
In frontend development, the browser is usually the primary client.
The client may also maintain temporary state, cache resources, and perform certain calculations.
A server is a system that provides services or resources to clients.
A web server can receive HTTP requests and return responses.
A server may run on a physical machine, a virtual machine, a container, or a serverless platform.
The term server describes the role of the system; it does not necessarily mean a single physical computer.
Consider a user attempting to sign in.
The user enters an email address and password in the frontend interface.
The application sends the credentials to an authentication endpoint using HTTPS.
The backend receives the submitted information.
The server checks the input and verifies the credentials using its authentication system.
The backend returns an appropriate success or failure response.
The frontend updates the interface depending on the result.
For example, the user may be redirected to the dashboard after successful authentication.
Importantly, the frontend must never be treated as the final authority for authentication or authorization. Security-sensitive decisions must be enforced by trusted server-side systems.
A basic two-tier architecture separates the client and the server.
The client communicates directly with the server responsible for processing requests and providing data or functionality.
This model is straightforward but may become difficult to maintain as application complexity increases.
A common web application architecture separates the system into three logical layers.
Handles what users see and interact with.
Handles business logic and application processing.
Handles persistent data storage and retrieval.
This separation improves maintainability, testing, and independent development.
Larger applications may introduce additional services and infrastructure components.
These components can be developed and deployed independently, depending on the architecture.
Client-server architecture also helps explain how frontend applications are rendered.
With client-side rendering, the browser downloads JavaScript and uses it to construct much of the user interface.

items: Server returns the HTML entry point and associated resources.
The application constructs and updates the interface.
Application logic can run in the browser.
Initial rendering may depend heavily on JavaScript.
Search engine visibility and initial loading behavior require careful implementation.
Large JavaScript bundles can affect performance.

blocks.text: With server-side rendering, the server generates HTML for a page and sends it to the browser.
The browser can display the returned HTML before the complete client-side application becomes interactive.

items: Faster initial content display in suitable scenarios.
Can improve search engine accessibility when correctly implemented.
Server rendering introduces additional architectural complexity.
Interactive features may still require client-side JavaScript.

blocks.text: With static site generation, HTML pages are generated ahead of time, often during a build process.
The generated files can then be delivered through a static hosting platform or CDN.

items: Reduced server-side processing for static content.
Useful for documentation, blogs, and course content.

blocks.text: Modern frameworks can combine these approaches.
Different pages or parts of an application may use static generation, server rendering, or client-side rendering depending on the requirements.
3.7 Why Frontend Engineers Must Understand Architecture
A frontend developer may encounter problems that cannot be solved by changing CSS or JavaScript alone.

items: An application has a CORS error.
A page works locally but fails after deployment.

blocks.text: Understanding architecture helps identify which component is responsible for a problem.

sections.title: LESSON 04 — HTTP, HTTPS and the Request-Response Lifecycle

blocks.text: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol.
It is an application-layer protocol used for communication between clients and servers.
Browsers use HTTP to request resources such as:
HTTP defines how requests and responses should be structured and interpreted.
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) identifies a resource and describes how to access it.
Identifies the protocol or access mechanism.
Identifies the destination port. The default HTTPS port is normally omitted from displayed URLs.
Identifies the requested resource or route.
Identifies a location or section within the resource. The fragment is generally processed by the browser rather than sent as part of the HTTP request to the server.
An HTTP request contains information describing what the client wants from the server.

GET /api/courses HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: ExampleBrowser
The request asks the server to retrieve the course information.
HTTP methods describe the intended action for a request.
The client requests the course list.
Used to submit data or request an operation that may create a resource.
Generally used to create or replace the state of a resource at a specified URI.
Used to apply a partial update to an existing resource.
Used to request the removal of a resource.
Other methods include HEAD, OPTIONS, CONNECT, and TRACE. Their behavior depends on the HTTP specification and application context.
Headers provide additional information about requests and responses.
Describes the media types the client can accept.
Describes the media type of the request body.
Carries authentication credentials or tokens according to the authentication scheme.
Identifies the client software in a format defined by the implementation.
Carries applicable cookies to the server.
Allows the server to set cookies.
Identifies another resource, commonly used during redirects.
Participates in controlling cross-origin access through CORS.
HTTP status codes communicate the outcome of a request.
Indicates that the request has been received and processing is continuing.

items: `201 Created` — A resource was successfully created.
`202 Accepted` — Request was accepted for processing.
`204 No Content` — Request completed successfully without a response body.
`301 Moved Permanently` — Resource has been assigned a new permanent URL.
`304 Not Modified` — The resource has not changed relative to the relevant cache validator.
`400 Bad Request` — The request cannot be processed because of a client-side request problem.
`401 Unauthorized` — Authentication is required or has failed.
`403 Forbidden` — The server refuses the requested operation.
`404 Not Found` — The requested resource could not be found.
`405 Method Not Allowed` — The method is not supported for that resource.
`429 Too Many Requests` — The client has exceeded a request limit.
`500 Internal Server Error` — An unexpected server failure occurred.
`502 Bad Gateway` — A gateway received an invalid response from an upstream server.
`503 Service Unavailable` — The server cannot currently handle the request.
`504 Gateway Timeout` — A gateway did not receive a timely upstream response.

blocks.text: Understanding status codes is essential when debugging frontend applications.
HTTPS is HTTP communication protected by Transport Layer Security (TLS).
It provides three important security properties:
Helps prevent unauthorized parties from reading information transmitted over the connection.
Helps detect unauthorized modification of information during transmission.
Allows the browser to verify the server's identity using its digital certificate and the certificate validation process.
HTTPS is particularly important for login forms, personal information, payments, and authenticated API communication.
HTTPS does not automatically make an application secure. Developers must still prevent application-level vulnerabilities, validate input, enforce authorization, and protect sensitive data.
4.8 Understanding TLS at a High Level
When a browser connects to an HTTPS website, it performs a TLS handshake.
The handshake allows the client and server to establish secure communication parameters and session keys.

items: The client initiates the connection and negotiates supported TLS options.
The browser validates the certificate chain, hostname, validity, and other relevant requirements.
The client and server establish shared cryptographic keys.

blocks.text: The exact handshake sequence differs depending on the TLS version and connection circumstances.
A typical lifecycle involves the following stages.
The browser interprets the entered URL and determines the destination hostname, scheme, and resource path.
The browser obtains an IP address for the domain, using cached information or DNS resolution.
The browser establishes the required transport connection.
For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 over TCP, this normally involves establishing a TCP connection.
For HTTP/3, QUIC is used instead.
For HTTPS, secure communication is established.
The browser sends a request containing the method, target, headers, and any applicable body.
The server receives the request and may perform several operations:
The server sends a response containing a status code, headers, and possibly a response body.
The browser interprets the returned content.
For an HTML document, it begins parsing the document and discovering additional resources.
The browser may request stylesheets, JavaScript files, images, fonts, and other resources.
The browser processes the document and styles, performs layout and painting, and displays the result.
This process is repeated as the user navigates or the application requests more information.
Caching stores copies of resources so they can be reused instead of repeatedly downloading them.
For example, a server can tell a browser that a particular static image may be reused for a specified period.
A browser may also send conditional requests to determine whether a cached resource has changed.
Understanding caching becomes especially important when deploying updated JavaScript, CSS, and frontend assets.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — DNS, Domains and Web Hosting Fundamentals

blocks.text: DNS stands for Domain Name System.
It translates human-readable domain names into information used by network clients, including IP addresses.
instead of remembering a numerical IP address.
DNS functions as a distributed naming system used across the internet.
Computers use network addresses to communicate, but remembering numerical addresses for every website would be inconvenient.
DNS provides a convenient mapping between domain names and network information.
It also allows an organization to change its hosting infrastructure without necessarily changing the domain name used by visitors.
The same domain name can resolve to different addresses depending on DNS configuration, resolver location, record type, and other circumstances.
The browser or operating system checks available cached DNS information.
If an appropriate result is not available, the configured DNS resolver may need to perform additional lookups.
The system checks whether it already knows the required DNS information.
The resolver attempts to obtain an answer for the requested hostname.
If necessary, the resolver asks the DNS root system where to find information about the relevant top-level domain.
The resolver follows the referral to the appropriate top-level domain DNS servers, such as those responsible for `.com`.
The resolver queries the authoritative DNS infrastructure for the domain.
The resolver returns the result to the client and may cache it according to its time-to-live rules.
This process is simplified. Actual resolution may involve caching, DNS forwarding, encrypted DNS, and other optimizations.
Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.
Creates an alias that points to another hostname.
A CNAME points to a hostname, not directly to an IP address.
Identifies mail servers responsible for receiving email for a domain.
Identifies authoritative name servers for a DNS zone.
A domain name is a human-readable name used to identify an internet resource or organization.
A domain can have multiple subdomains.
Different subdomains can point to different services or infrastructure.
Domain registration is the process of registering a domain name through a registrar.
The registrar provides the administrative service that allows the registrant to manage the registered domain.
Domain ownership and DNS hosting are related but separate responsibilities.

items: A registrar manages the domain registration.
A DNS provider manages DNS records.
A hosting provider runs the website or application.

blocks.text: One company may provide all three services, but they do not have to be operated by the same company.
Web hosting provides the infrastructure required to make website files or application services accessible over a network.
Different hosting approaches serve different needs.
Multiple websites share resources on a hosting server.

items: Performance may vary depending on other hosted workloads.

blocks.text: A VPS provides an isolated virtual server environment.

items: Security updates and server configuration may become the user's responsibility.

blocks.text: A dedicated server provides an entire physical server for a particular customer or workload.
Cloud hosting uses virtualized and distributed infrastructure to run applications.
Static hosting serves prebuilt files such as:
It is commonly used for frontend applications and static websites.
Serverless platforms execute application code without requiring developers to manage traditional server infrastructure directly.
They commonly support event-driven or request-driven workloads.
Serverless does not mean that servers do not exist. It means that the hosting provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure.
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) distributes content through a network of geographically distributed locations.
Instead of every visitor downloading resources from one distant origin server, a CDN may serve cached resources from a location closer to the visitor.

items: Better handling of distributed user traffic.

blocks.text: A CDN may also provide additional services such as TLS termination, DDoS protection, and traffic routing.
5.9 Putting Domains, DNS, Hosting, and CDNs Together
Consider a frontend application hosted through a cloud platform.

items: A user enters the domain name.
DNS resolves the domain to the appropriate network destination.
The visitor connects to the hosting or edge infrastructure.
The hosting platform returns the application files.
A CDN may deliver cached static assets.
The frontend communicates with backend APIs when needed.

blocks.text: A well-designed application may use one provider for domain registration, another for DNS, another for frontend hosting, and a separate platform for backend services.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — How Browsers Load and Render Web Pages

blocks.text: A web browser is a software application that retrieves, processes, and displays web content.
A browser is much more than a window that displays websites.
It contains multiple internal systems responsible for:
Different browsers use different internal implementations, but they follow common web platform standards.
A simplified browser architecture includes the following components.
The browser's main process coordinates browser-level functionality.
It manages activities such as tabs, navigation, permissions, and communication with other processes.
Responsible for retrieving resources from the internet.
It handles HTTP communication, caching, connections, and network-related behavior.
Processes HTML and CSS and participates in converting documents into visible content.
For example, Chromium-based browsers use Blink, while Firefox uses Gecko.

items: V8 is used by Chromium-based browsers.

blocks.text: These components help combine rendered content into the final displayed image.
They may use GPU acceleration for supported operations.
Suppose a user visits a webpage containing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.
The browser typically performs the following work.
The browser begins navigating to the requested URL.
The browser obtains the HTML document and discovers additional resources.
The browser parses HTML and constructs the Document Object Model (DOM).
The browser downloads and parses CSS and constructs the CSS Object Model (CSSOM).
The browser processes and executes JavaScript according to script loading and execution rules.
JavaScript can modify the DOM and styles, and certain scripts can affect how HTML parsing progresses.
The browser combines relevant document and style information to determine what needs to be rendered.
The browser calculates the geometry and position of rendered elements.
The browser determines how visual content should be drawn.
The browser combines the appropriate visual layers to produce the final display.
These activities can overlap and repeat. A page is not necessarily processed in one simple, strictly sequential pass.
The browser parses HTML and builds a structured representation of the document.

Welcome to the Web

Learn how browsers work.
The browser identifies elements, attributes, text nodes, and their relationships.
It uses this structure to construct the DOM.
CSS describes the presentation of HTML elements.
The browser parses CSS and determines which declarations apply to which elements.
The CSS Object Model (CSSOM) represents the browser's parsed CSS rules and related style information.
JavaScript can add behavior and modify the webpage.

const heading = document.querySelector("h1");

heading.textContent = "Understanding Browser Rendering";
This code selects the heading and changes its text.
The browser detects the DOM change and updates the relevant visual output.
JavaScript execution and browser rendering interact closely, so inefficient scripts or excessive DOM changes can affect responsiveness.
These are important stages of browser rendering.
The browser calculates the dimensions and positions of elements.

items: How wide is a content container?
Where should a navigation bar appear?
How much space should a heading occupy?
How should grid columns be distributed?

blocks.text: Painting determines how visual properties are drawn.
The browser combines visual layers into the final display.
Some visual operations can be handled efficiently through compositing, depending on the browser and the properties being animated.
Poorly designed frontend code can force the browser to perform unnecessary work.
For example, repeatedly changing the dimensions of many elements can cause expensive layout calculations.
Large images can increase download time and memory use.
A frontend engineer should understand browser rendering to build websites that are responsive and efficient.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — Understanding the DOM, CSSOM and Render Tree

blocks.text: DOM stands for Document Object Model.
It is a programming interface that represents a document as a tree of objects.
The browser constructs the DOM when it parses HTML.
JavaScript can access and modify it.

Document
└── html
    └── body
        └── main
            ├── h1
            │   └── "Frontend Engineering"
            └── p
                └── "Build modern web applications."
Each element represents a node in the document tree.
Represents an HTML element such as `div`, `p`, or `button`.
Elements also expose their attributes through DOM interfaces.
JavaScript provides several ways to select and manipulate elements.
This selects the first matching heading.
This selects all elements matching the class.

const image = document.querySelector("img");

image.setAttribute("alt", "Frontend course illustration");
These operations demonstrate how JavaScript can change the document dynamically.
Events allow JavaScript to respond to user actions and browser activity.
The browser detects the click and invokes the registered callback.
Understanding events is essential for building interactive frontend applications.
CSSOM stands for CSS Object Model.
It represents parsed CSS rules and provides interfaces for accessing and manipulating CSS information.
The browser uses CSS information to determine how elements should be styled.
The browser parses these declarations and determines their applicable styles.
JavaScript can also interact with the CSSOM.
This changes the element's inline style.
The browser then updates its rendering as required.
The render tree is an internal representation used during browser rendering.
It combines relevant document structure and computed styling information to determine the visual objects that need to be displayed.
The render tree is related to, but not identical to, the DOM.
The hidden paragraph remains part of the DOM.
However, an element with `display: none` does not generate a normal visual box in the render tree.
This illustrates why the DOM and rendered output are not identical.
7.7 DOM vs CSSOM vs Render Tree
| DOM | Represents document structure and content |
| CSSOM | Represents parsed CSS rules and style information |
| Render tree | Represents visual content needed for rendering |
All three concepts contribute to the browser's rendering process, but they represent different information.
Changing an element can cause the browser to perform additional rendering work.
Reflow refers to recalculating layout information.
Changes that may cause layout include:
Repainting refers to redrawing visual content.
Certain changes can require painting without changing the layout geometry.
The exact rendering work depends on the property, implementation, and other affected elements.
Frontend developers should avoid unnecessary rendering work.

items: Batch related DOM modifications when appropriate.
Avoid excessive layout reads and writes that can force synchronous layout.
Use CSS transitions and animations thoughtfully.
Prefer animating properties that can often be efficiently composited, such as `transform` and `opacity`.
Use event delegation when many similar elements require event handling.
Remove event listeners and clean up resources when they are no longer needed.

blocks.text: These techniques become increasingly important when developing large applications.

sections.title: LESSON 08 — Frontend Development Environments and Developer Tools

blocks.text: A frontend development environment is the collection of software and tools used to build, run, test, debug, and maintain web applications.
Setting up a consistent environment improves productivity and reduces avoidable development problems.
A code editor provides an environment for writing and organizing source code.
Frontend developers should become comfortable navigating codebases, searching files, reading errors, and using keyboard shortcuts.
JavaScript was originally designed to run inside web browsers.
Runtime environments also allow JavaScript to execute outside browsers.
Node.js is a widely used JavaScript runtime.
Frontend development tools often depend on Node.js to run:
A runtime is not the same thing as a frontend framework.
A package manager helps developers install, update, remove, and manage project dependencies.
Installs the dependencies declared by the project.
Runs the development script configured in `package.json`, when such a script exists.
Runs the project's production build script.
Runs the configured test script, when available.
A typical `package.json` file describes a JavaScript project.
The actual package versions and scripts depend on the project.
A frontend project may use a structure such as:

frontend-project/
│
├── public/
│   └── favicon.ico
│
├── src/
│   ├── assets/
│   ├── components/
│   ├── pages/
│   ├── services/
│   ├── styles/
│   ├── App.jsx
│   └── main.jsx
│
├── package.json
├── index.html
└── vite.config.js
This is an example, not a mandatory structure.
Contains files served as static assets.
May contain API communication and other service logic.
Contains CSS and related styling files.
Provides the HTML entry point for many frontend build tools.
Browser developer tools are among the most important tools for frontend engineers.
They allow developers to inspect and debug applications directly in the browser.
Inspect and modify the DOM and CSS.
Displays JavaScript messages, warnings, and errors.
It can also execute JavaScript expressions.
Allows developers to inspect and debug JavaScript source files.
Helps investigate runtime performance and rendering behavior.
Provides information about browser-side application storage and related features.
Depending on the browser, this may include:
Developer tools can emulate different screen sizes and device conditions.
Responsive design is not simply shrinking a desktop interface. It involves arranging content so that it remains usable across screen sizes.
A systematic debugging process is more effective than changing random lines of code.
For example, suppose a course list does not appear.

items: Open the Console and inspect JavaScript errors.
Check the request URL and method.
Check whether the frontend receives the expected data.
Check whether CSS is hiding or incorrectly positioning the content.

blocks.text: This process helps identify whether the issue exists in the frontend, backend, network, or rendering layer.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — Git, GitHub and Frontend Project Workflows

blocks.text: Version control is a system for recording and managing changes to files over time.

items: Identify when a bug was introduced.

blocks.text: Version control is essential for modern software development.
Git is a distributed version-control system.
Each Git repository contains project history and version-control information.
Developers can work locally, create branches, commit changes, and exchange repository updates with other repositories.

items: Local development without requiring continuous network access.
Recovery from many types of mistakes.

blocks.text: GitHub is a platform for hosting Git repositories and collaborating on software projects.
Git and GitHub are not the same.
Git is the version-control system. GitHub is one platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features.
A repository contains project files and version-control history.
The working directory contains the files you are currently modifying.
The staging area contains changes selected for the next commit.
A commit records a snapshot of selected changes.
A branch provides an independent line of development.
A merge integrates changes from different development histories.
A remote is a reference to another repository, often hosted on GitHub.
A pull request is a collaboration mechanism used to propose changes and request review before merging them into a target branch.
Start by checking the repository state:
Push changes to a remote branch:
This example assumes the remote is named `origin` and the branch is named `main`.
In shared projects, developers should review their staged changes before committing rather than automatically staging every modified file.
Cloning creates a local copy of a remote repository.
Install its dependencies using the project's documented package manager:
Start the development server using the available project script:
Branches allow developers to work on features independently.
When feature development is complete, changes can be pushed and reviewed through a pull request.
A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically combine competing changes.

items: Developer A modifies a component's rendering logic.
Developer B modifies the same section of the same component.

blocks.text: Git may require a developer to decide how those changes should be combined.
A conflict does not automatically mean that code has been lost.

items: Understand the purpose of both changes.

blocks.text: Never resolve conflicts by blindly accepting all changes from one side without reviewing what will be lost.

sections.title: PRACTICAL LAB — Inspect Browser Network Requests, Rendering Behavior and the Structure of a Real Website

blocks.text: Investigate how a real website works internally by using browser developer tools.
You will inspect its document structure, styles, network communication, resource loading, and rendering behavior.
This lab connects the theoretical concepts from all nine lessons.

items: Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, or another browser with developer tools.
A code editor for recording observations.

blocks.text: Use a website you are permitted to inspect. Do not attempt to access restricted endpoints, private information, or systems without authorization.

items: Open a website in your browser.
Identify headings, paragraphs, links, images, buttons, and navigation elements.

blocks.text: **Expected understanding:** The visible webpage is represented by a structured DOM rather than being one flat image.
Experiment 2 — Inspect CSS and Computed Styles

items: Select a heading inside the Elements panel.
Examine its final font size, color, dimensions, and spacing.
Which stylesheet defines the element's appearance.
How the browser applies the cascade.
How changing CSS affects visual output.

blocks.text: **Expected understanding:** The browser combines multiple CSS declarations to determine the computed appearance of an element.

items: Enable Preserve log if you want to retain requests during navigation.
Observe the requests generated by the browser.
Examine its Headers and Response sections.
Select a stylesheet or JavaScript file.
Compare its request and response information.

blocks.text: **Expected understanding:** A webpage is usually assembled from multiple resources downloaded through network requests.
Choose an appropriate network request and inspect its response headers.
Not every response will contain every header.
Compare response headers with the content returned by the server.
**Expected understanding:** HTTP headers provide additional information about how a resource should be interpreted, cached, or handled.
**Expected understanding:** JavaScript can interact with the DOM and change the webpage without downloading an entirely new HTML document.

items: Open the Device Toolbar in developer tools.
Observe how navigation, text, images, and columns change.

blocks.text: **Expected understanding:** Responsive web design uses flexible layouts and CSS rules to adapt interfaces to different viewport sizes.

items: Stop the recording after the initial load.
Examine JavaScript activity and rendering-related events.

blocks.text: **Expected understanding:** Browser performance depends on more than downloading files. Parsing, scripting, layout, painting, and other activities contribute to the user experience.
Experiment 8 — Inspect DNS and Connection Information

items: Observe available phases such as DNS lookup, connection establishment, SSL/TLS negotiation, request sending, and waiting.
Compare these timings with the overall request duration.

blocks.text: Some phases may be absent or reused because the browser may already have cached DNS information or an existing network connection.
**Expected understanding:** Website access depends on name resolution, connection establishment, secure communication, and server response.
Prepare a short technical report containing:

items: The website inspected and the date of inspection.
A screenshot of the page's DOM structure.
A screenshot of the computed CSS for one selected element.
Five network requests with their methods, status codes, and resource types.
The response headers of the main HTML document.
An example of a DOM modification using JavaScript.
Observations from three different viewport sizes.
A brief explanation of the performance recording.
A description of the request-response lifecycle observed during the experiment.

blocks.text: Do not include private information, authentication tokens, session cookies, or other sensitive request data in the report.

Developer tools help engineers inspect network requests, DOM structure, styles, and performance.
Git and GitHub support version control and collaborative development.

You should be able to explain how a browser retrieves a website, how the server responds, how the browser processes the returned resources, and how the resulting interface appears on the screen.
You should also be able to independently inspect a real website using browser developer tools and explain the major steps involved in its loading and rendering process.
**Next Module:** HTML5 — Semantic Structure, Forms and Modern Web Document Engineering.

**Important course-design note:** This module deliberately establishes the web architecture foundation before moving into HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, and modern frontend frameworks. It gives students the context needed to understand not just *how to write frontend code*, but *how that code works inside a real browser and web application*.
